lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Pedro Monaco | Lesson 10 -- Compliance and the Cost of Getting It Wrong
phases: The Cost of Getting It Wrong

paras: Read enough enforcement reports and you notice that they all have the same shape. There is a rule. There is a process that was supposed to apply the rule. There is a moment, usually eighteen months before anybody outside the company hears about it, when somebody could have looked and did not. And then there is a number: a fine, a settlement, and a paragraph in which nobody admits wrongdoing. The number is what gets reported. The moment is what the report is actually about.

What is striking, once you have read a few, is how rarely anything was concealed. The classic case is not a conspiracy. It is a control that existed on paper, an audit that was scheduled and postponed twice, and a red flag that sat in a queue because the person who could have escalated it had been given four hundred other things to look at that quarter. If the audit had happened in the second year, the whole thing would have cost a conversation. It happened in the fourth, by which time it cost a percentage of global revenue.

The arithmetic is not subtle, and it is the reason regulators keep saying the same thing. Disclosing early is almost always cheaper than explaining late. Companies that go to the regulator themselves get credit for it, in most systems explicitly and in all of them informally. Companies that are found get the penalty and the reputational damage, and the second one does not have a number attached to it, which is exactly why it is underweighted in the meeting where somebody decides to wait and see.

So the useful question after any failure is not who is to blame. It is which of the things that did not happen would have changed the outcome, and which would not. If the control had been tested rather than written, this would not be happening. If the second audit had gone ahead, we would know how long it had been going on. If somebody had been given the time to read the queue, they would have seen it. Those are three different repairs with three different costs, and a company that cannot tell them apart tends to buy the most expensive one and fix nothing.

listenings.text: People expect this work to be dramatic and it almost never is. In fifteen years I have opened a great many files and found a conspiracy perhaps twice. What I find the rest of the time is an email that somebody read on a Friday, a control that was written down and never tested, and an audit that got moved twice because the quarter was busy. If that audit had gone ahead the first time it was scheduled, most of these cases would not exist. That is not a comforting thing to tell a board, because a conspiracy is somebody else's fault and a postponed audit is theirs. The sentence I have said most often in my career is this: nothing was concealed here, nobody looked. And if somebody had been given four hours and permission, they would have found it in an afternoon.

The cheapest lesson any organisation ever gets is the one where nothing happened. Somebody notices a payment that should not have been possible, it gets stopped, and the whole thing is over in a morning. That is a free education, and almost nobody takes it, because there is no damage to explain and therefore no meeting. If we treated near misses the way aviation does, half of what I work on would never reach me. Aviation writes them up whether or not anybody was hurt, and the write-up goes to people who were not involved. We do the opposite: we investigate in proportion to the harm, so the only lessons that get learned are the expensive ones. If our industry had adopted that habit twenty years ago, the fines we are still paying for would look very different. It costs nothing. That is precisely why it never gets funded.

extra_audio.text: A rule exists, and a process is written down to apply it. The audit that would have tested that process is scheduled and then postponed twice. A red flag arrives and sits in the queue of somebody with four hundred other things to read. Eighteen months later the regulator finds it, and nothing had been concealed at any point. A fine is paid, nobody admits wrongdoing, and the reputational damage has no number attached to it.
